questions.q: How many Hebrew letters have a second shape used at the end of a word?
questions.why: Five: כ מ נ פ צ. They are not extra letters and the list never grows, so once you know these five you know every final form there is.

questions.q: Which of these is the final form of נ?
questions.why: נוּן סוֹפִית is ן, a stroke that drops below the line. That descender is also what keeps it apart from ו, which sits on the line and has no final form at all.

questions.q: Put the five final letters into alef-bet order.
questions.why: ך ם ן ף ץ, the order of כ מ נ פ צ in the alef-bet. Israeli schoolchildren hold the set with the nonsense word כַּמְנַפֵּץ, which spells all five in exactly this order.

questions.q: Why is it מֶלֶךְ with ך but מַלְכָּה with כ?
choices: The כ is the last letter of the first word and not of the second
A feminine word never takes a final letter
The dagesh in מַלְכָּה blocks the final form
מַלְכָּה is borrowed and keeps a foreign spelling
questions.why: A letter wears its final shape only while it is last. Add anything after it, a suffix included, and it goes straight back to its ordinary shape: כֶּלֶב becomes כְּלָבִים and the ב never had a choice either.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for money. It ends in a final letter.
questions.why: It ends in ף, the final form of פ, and the sound is /f/ because there is no dagesh in it. Written mid-word the same letter would be פ, as in מִשְׁפָּחָה.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for a son.
questions.why: Two letters, and the second is ן rather than נ because it is last. This is the shortest possible demonstration of the rule, and a useful one to picture when you are unsure.
Wine, /yayin/. It opens with י as a consonant and closes with final ן, so the same word shows a letter that never changes shape next to one that always does at the end.

questions.q: What tells ן and ו apart in print?
choices: ן drops below the line and ו sits on it
ן is longer at the top
Nothing; you guess from the word
questions.why: Both are a single vertical stroke, and the descender is the whole difference. It matters most in handwriting, where the shapes get closer still, and knowing that ו has no final form removes half the guesswork: a lone stroke at the end of a word is usually ן.
Now, /akhshav/. It ends in ו, which looks like a candidate for a final form and is not: only those five letters change, and וָו has one shape wherever it stands.

questions.q: Which of these words is spelled wrongly?
questions.why: A צ at the end of a word must be ץ, so it is אֶרֶץ. Mid-word it stays צ, as in מִצְוָוה. This course marks a slip like this as correct and then shows you the proper spelling, because the sound is identical and the habit is what needs fixing.
Needs to, must, /tsarikh/. It opens with צ and closes with ך, and the ך has no dagesh so it is /kh/ rather than /k/: the final form and the soft sound often arrive together at the end of a word.

questions.q: Type the plural of the Hebrew word for a book.
questions.why: The plural ending ־ִים lands after the ר, so nothing in the word is last except the מ, which therefore must be ם. The ר has no final form to worry about in the first place.

questions.q: Which of these is true of handwritten Hebrew?
choices: It has the same five final letters, in the same places
It has two more final letters than print
Israelis write the nikud by hand as well
questions.why: The shapes change but the system does not: handwriting keeps all five finals. What handwriting drops is the nikud, which is a printing convention for dictionaries, poetry and courses, never something an adult writes in a note.

questions.q: State the rule about where a final letter may appear, and give one word pair that shows a letter losing its final shape.
a: A final form appears only as the very last letter of a word, never at the start, never in the middle, and never before a suffix written onto the same word. כֶּלֶב a dog becomes כְּלָבִים dogs: once ־ִים is added the ב is no longer last. מֶלֶךְ against מַלְכָּה shows the same thing with כ.
questions.why: The rule is positional, not lexical: it is about where the letter stands in the word today, not about which word it belongs to. That is why adding a plural or a suffix can change the spelling of a letter that nobody touched.
